images.title: Bigger number, shorter list
images.purpose: Show the counterexample to Anshu's claim: 121 is bigger than 96 yet has a shorter prime factorisation.
images.composition: Two horizontal rows of prime tiles, one above the other, left aligned so the lengths can be compared at a glance, with a short caption below.
exact_structure: Top row: the label 96 then exactly 6 teal #0072B2 tiles: 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3; to the right the note 6 primes.
Bottom row: the label 121 then exactly 2 amber #E69F00 tiles: 11, 11; to the right the note 2 primes.
All tiles the same size, so the 96 row is visibly three times as long as the 121 row.
A reddish purple #CC79A7 bracket beside the 121 label with the caption Bigger number, shorter factorisation.
One word under everything in vermilion #D55E00: Counterexample.
rejection: the 96 row with a tile count other than 6, or with other than five 2s and one 3
the 121 row with a tile count other than 2
tiles drawn at different sizes so the length comparison is misleading
images.takeaway: One counterexample is enough to show a claim is false.
images.description: Six tiles for 96 (five 2s and a 3) above two tiles for 121 (11 and 11), labelled as a counterexample.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video on Anshu's claim and counterexamples.
images.teaching_notes: Compare the row lengths first, then the numbers, to see that size and length do not match.

image_decisions.why: Tile rows of different lengths make the counterexample obvious without reading.
